subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Green Defaults for Energy
description: A quick win: understand Green Defaults for Energy.

hook.text: Germany offered green energy as the default. Over 90% of customers stayed on it.

buildup.text: Green defaults enroll people in renewable energy plans and let them opt out to conventional sources if they prefer.

discovery.text: Pichert and Katsikopoulos found that green defaults are the single most effective tool for increasing renewable energy.

twist.text: Critics argue people pay more without realizing it. But the opt-out is easy and most who switch back do so for price.

climax.text: Green defaults show that environmental behavior isn't mainly about values. It's about what's set up for you.

punchline.text: Want a greener world? Change the default.

quiz.question: What makes green defaults effective?
options: They force people to use only renewable energy
Most people don't switch away from whatever is pre-selected

details.summary: Green defaults set environmentally friendly options as the pre-selected choice for energy contracts, appliance settings, and building systems. Since most people accept defaults, green defaults can dramatically shift aggregate environmental impact without restricting anyone's choices.
details.whyItMatters: Green defaults leverage inertia for environmental benefit at minimal cost. When renewable energy is the default power source or double-sided printing is the default setting, the vast majority of users stick with the green option, producing massive.
takeaways: Setting green energy as the default shifts most consumers to renewable sources
Double-sided printing defaults save enormous amounts of paper in organizations
Green defaults work because most people accept defaults regardless of content

faq.question: How effective are green defaults compared to green incentives?
faq.answer: Green defaults typically achieve 80 to 90 percent adoption compared to 10 to 20 percent for incentive programs. The behavioral inertia that keeps people at the default is far more powerful than financial incentives at shifting aggregate behavior.

faq.question: Is it ethical to default people into green energy options?
faq.answer: Libertarian paternalism says yes, because people can opt out freely and the default serves both individual and collective benefit. Critics argue that the nudge exploits inertia to impose the choice architect's values. Transparency about the default is important for legitimacy.
